entries.concept: Namespace and label conventions for production
entries.description: Create a dedicated Namespace for each environment or team with labels: environment, managed-by, team. Standard labels applied to all resources: app (service name), version (semver), environment. Namespaces provide resource isolation, RBAC scope, and NetworkPolicy boundaries.
decision_rules: Use one namespace per environment (production, staging, development) — do not mix environments
Apply consistent labels (app, version, environment) to all resources to enable selectors and monitoring
Set managed-by: terraform or managed-by: helm on namespaces created via IaC
tradeoffs: Fine-grained namespace-per-team increases isolation but requires more RBAC and NetworkPolicy configuration
anti_patterns: Deploying production workloads to the default namespace
Omitting labels — makes resource selection, monitoring dashboards, and GitOps tooling fragile
aws_alignment: EKS namespaces map to IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) scope for granular AWS API access control

entries.description: Production Deployment: 3 replicas, RollingUpdate strategy (maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 for zero-downtime), dedicated ServiceAccount (automountServiceAccountToken: false), podAntiAffinity across nodes, pod-level SecurityContext (runAsNonRoot, seccompProfile RuntimeDefault), container-level SecurityContext (allowPrivilegeEscalation: false, readOnlyRootFilesystem: true, capabilities drop ALL), resource requests/limits, env from ConfigMap/Secret, liveness + readiness + startup probes, emptyDir volumes for writable paths, terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 60.
decision_rules: Set maxUnavailable: 0 for zero-downtime rolling deployments — pods are added before old ones are removed
Use pinned image tags (myapp:1.0.0) — never :latest in production
Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds >= timeout of your longest in-flight request to allow graceful shutdown
tradeoffs: maxUnavailable: 0 requires cluster capacity for maxSurge extra pods during rollout
podAntiAffinity with preferredDuringScheduling may not spread pods if cluster nodes are insufficient
anti_patterns: Using :latest image tag — non-deterministic and bypasses rollback capability
Not setting terminationGracePeriodSeconds — pods may be killed mid-request
Missing startup probe for slow-starting apps — liveness probe will kill the pod before it finishes initializing
aws_alignment: Use Karpenter on EKS for just-in-time node provisioning to support rolling surge capacity

entries.description: Service type ClusterIP on port 80 -> targetPort 8000. Never NodePort or LoadBalancer directly for internal services. Ingress with nginx ingress class, cert-manager annotation (letsencrypt-prod), ssl-redirect: true, proxy-body-size: 10m, rate-limit: 100. TLS spec with hosts array and secretName for certificate.
decision_rules: Use ClusterIP as the default Service type — expose externally only via Ingress
Set nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rate-limit on all public-facing Ingress resources
Use cert-manager with Let's Encrypt for automated TLS certificate management
tradeoffs: Nginx Ingress with rate-limit annotation is per-server, not distributed — use Redis-backed rate limiting for distributed enforcement
anti_patterns: Using NodePort or direct LoadBalancer Service types without an Ingress — bypasses centralized TLS and rate limiting
Not setting proxy-body-size — allows unbounded request body sizes
aws_alignment: On EKS, use AWS Load Balancer Controller with Ingress class alb for native ALB integration and ACM certificate management

entries.concept: Horizontal Pod Autoscaler (HPA) for automatic scaling
entries.description: HPA (autoscaling/v2): scaleTargetRef points to the Deployment, minReplicas: 2, maxReplicas: 10. Metrics: CPU target utilization 70%, Memory target utilization 80%. Kubernetes scales pod count up/down to maintain the target metric values.
decision_rules: Set minReplicas >= 2 for production availability — 1 replica has no fault tolerance
Use CPU utilization 70% as a target — leaves headroom before pods become saturated
Combine HPA with PodDisruptionBudget to prevent all replicas from being disrupted simultaneously
tradeoffs: HPA reacts to current load — not suitable for sudden traffic spikes; use KEDA for event-driven scaling
Memory-based scaling can cause scale-thrash if memory is not released promptly after load drops
anti_patterns: Setting minReplicas: 1 in production — a single pod disruption causes a complete outage
Setting maxReplicas too high without resource quotas — a runaway HPA can exhaust cluster capacity
aws_alignment: Combine HPA with Karpenter on EKS for both pod and node autoscaling
Use KEDA with SQS queue depth metric for event-driven HPA on EKS

entries.description: ConfigMap holds non-sensitive configuration: APP_ENV, LOG_LEVEL, CORS_ORIGINS, MAX_CONNECTIONS. Secrets hold sensitive values (DATABASE_URL) but in production should be managed via External Secrets Operator, not committed as plain Secret manifests. Reference ConfigMap values with valueFrom.configMapKeyRef, Secrets with valueFrom.secretKeyRef.
decision_rules: ConfigMap is for non-sensitive configuration only — never put passwords or tokens in ConfigMap
In production: use External Secrets Operator to sync from AWS Secrets Manager into Kubernetes Secrets
Reference individual keys (configMapKeyRef, secretKeyRef) rather than envFrom for explicit env var declarations
tradeoffs: envFrom (whole ConfigMap/Secret as env vars) is simpler but makes pod environment unpredictable — prefer key-by-key references
anti_patterns: Storing sensitive values in ConfigMap data (not encrypted at rest by default)
Committing Secret manifests with base64-encoded values to git — base64 is encoding, not encryption
aws_alignment: Use External Secrets Operator with AWS Secrets Manager SecretStore for EKS
Use Secrets Store CSI Driver with AWS SSM Parameter Store as an alternative
